[CGK+20], and $\widetilde{O}((m/\varepsilon)^{2/3})$, a consequence of their results and those of Clifford, Kociumaka, and Porat [CKP18]. For $\varepsilon=Θ(m^{-a})$, the better of our two bounds improves on both prior space exponents for every fixed $0<a<1/2$. A Fourier matcher uses $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}(m/K)^2)$ words to estimate each distance $d$ within $\varepsilon(d+K)$, giving relative error at most $2\varepsilon$ for $d\ge K$. A threshold matcher based on random-prime residue refinements and the multi-stream dictionary matching algorithm of Golan, Kopelowitz, and Porat [GKP18] gives our second space bound directly. Combining it with the Fourier matcher gives the first. Both space bounds extend to $L_1$ matching over polynomially bounded integer symbols.

papers.title: Inferring Neural Activity Changes under Recording Uncertainty with Transformers and Variational Inference
papers.abstract: A difference in recorded firing rate across days may reflect a change in neuronal activity, missed spikes or recording a different neuron. We present a statistical approach that combines neuron tracking with Bayesian estimates of stationary mean recorded firing rates. Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

papers.title: A boundary integral formulation for microscale Marangoni surfing
papers.abstract: We consider a model for collections of surfactant-producing particles moving along the surface of a viscous fluid under their self-generated Marangoni flows. Such systems are challenging due to their nonlocal nature: particle motion is coupled to Marangoni stresses distributed across the entire fluid surface and to the resulting flows in the bulk. In the low Reynolds and Péclet number limit, we reduce these nonlocal effects to a system of integral equations supported solely on the particles and their boundaries. This formulation is not only computationally tractable, but also provides a framework for systematically coarse-graining many-particle systems. Numerical simulations, performed with a custom spectral method, show collective dynamics are highly sensitive to shape. In particular, among elliptical particles, we find prolate particles tend to attract while oblate particles tend to repel, and these geometric details control the stability of polarized populations. We rationalize these behaviors through a far-field expansion of the boundary integral equations and its corresponding reduced-order model.

papers.title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
papers.abstract: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.

papers.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
papers.abstract: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

papers.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
papers.abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

papers.title: A$^3$Bench: Compositional Reasoning over Aggressive Interactions in Videos
papers.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: https://github.com/austincbaker/A3Bench.

papers.title: A Lions lift framework for gradient and Newtonian evolutions in Wasserstein spaces
papers.abstract: To analyze evolutions driven by functionals over the space of probability measures, one can opt for the extrinsic Lions lift approach or the intrinsic Wasserstein viewpoint with its abstract metric structure. While the latter has been a successful playground for the study of first-order gradient flows, it classically relies on $λ$-convexity, and has eluded attempts of extensions to second-order Newtonian-like dynamics. Motivated by these obstructions, we show that the extrinsic Lions lift has the full capabilities to carry out the first-order gradient-flow program, which is classically done intrinsically in the Wasserstein space. As illustrated in an example, this paves the way for a framework of gradient evolutions beyond the $λ$-convex case, which is classically demanded for energies in the Wasserstein space. Furthermore, our interpretation of the Lions lift enables the formulation of a notion of second-order Newtonian curves in the Wasserstein phase space. Such curves can be constructed through a second-order JKO-like scheme and, when applied to linear and interacting energies, naturally lead to Vlasov kinetic equations and existence of solutions thereof.

papers.title: Quadratic splitting for a weighted Monge--Ampère equation on $(0,\infty)^l\times\R^m$
papers.abstract: We study a Monge--Ampère equation arising from the existence problem for complete Kähler--Einstein metrics with zero Ricci curvature on divisor complements. We prove a splitting theorem for nonnegative smooth strictly convex solutions on a product of positive half lines and a Euclidean space. The potential and its first derivatives extend continuously to the boundary. The directional derivative in the equation is positive in the interior and vanishes on the boundary. After an affine change of variables, the solution is the sum of a function on the product of half lines and a positive definite quadratic form in the Euclidean variables. No growth condition or homogeneity is assumed.

papers.title: Characterizing adsorption thermodynamics in carbon capture materials: an efficient first-principles approach
papers.abstract: Porous materials offer a vast design space for CO$_2$ capture, whose exploration hinges on efficient and accurate first-principles predictions of the thermodynamics governing adsorption. However, simulating isotherms and heats of adsorption using grand canonical molecular simulations is extremely computationally expensive when combined with accurate ab initio treatments of the molecular interactions, limiting screening to low-pressure uptake encoded in the Henry constant. Identifying and designing the best CO$_2$ capture materials requires a strategy that can efficiently calculate their adsorption properties using ab initio potential energy surfaces such as those now available from foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Here we develop a neural classical density functional (cDFT) framework for carbon capture processes that allows direct calculation of adsorption isotherms from low to high loading limits of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) without grand canonical simulations. We demonstrate the success of our approach by calculating the ab initio adsorption isotherms for over 5,000 experimentally reported MOFs. From our screening, we show how these materials can be characterized using four isotherm shapes, arising from their pore size and binding sites, which the Henry constant cannot distinguish. We show that these shapes, rather than the binding strength alone, decide which MOFs suit which process: small pores with strong binding sites for vacuum and temperature swings at low pressure, large pores with weakly binding walls for pressure swings. Finally, we identify the most promising candidates by weighing their working capacity against the energy needed for regeneration.

papers.title: Polycentrality in Urban Socioecological Systems: A Multilayer Analysis of Social Infrastructure in Iztapalapa, Mexico City
papers.abstract: The spatial distribution of infrastructure and activities, along with the networks and interactions that connect them, is key to understanding the relationship between urban form, function, and sustainability from a complex systems perspective. Within this dynamic relationship, the extent to which localized social infrastructure can reinforce existing functional centralities or create conditions for the emergence of new ones remains insufficiently understood. This study examines these relationships through the UTOPÍAS program in Iztapalapa, Mexico City, where 15 public social facilities have been established across a historically underserved urban territory. We develop a multilayer network framework integrating pedestrian infrastructure, GTFS-based public transport services, and UTOPÍAS as a target layer to assess multimodal connectivity, travel-time accessibility, and spatial coverage. These conditions are examined alongside indicators of local economic centrality (PCI and wPCI) to investigate how infrastructure interdependencies relate to the functional organization of urban space. The analysis reveals spatial heterogeneity in multimodal accessibility and differences in the integration of UTOPÍAS with existing transport networks. By relating these patterns to pre-existing economic centralities, we examine whether distributed social infrastructure may reinforce established functional centers or create conditions favorable to emerging centralities, without assuming that spatial decentralization necessarily produces polycentrality. The findings contribute a relational, data-driven approach to understanding how social infrastructure and mobility shape urban functions, emphasizing accessibility and territorial integration as critical conditions for more equitable and sustainable urban development.

papers.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
papers.abstract: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

papers.title: Exponential boundary stabilization of the KdV--KdV system with time-varying delay: the nonlinear case
papers.abstract: We consider a Boussinesq system of KdV--KdV type on a bounded interval, with a boundary feedback that includes a damping term with a time-varying delayed term. Although the exponential stability of the linearized system was established in [1] by a Lyapunov approach, global existence and stabilization for the nonlinear problem remained open. Here, we prove that, for sufficiently small initial data and under a suitable restriction on the interval length, the nonlinear system admits a unique global solution whose energy decays exponentially. In particular, we provide an explicit decay rate and a quantitative smallness condition on the initial energy. Our approach combines a Lyapunov argument with well-posedness estimates that are uniform under time translations of the delay, allowing the solutions to be continued globally.

papers.title: Grain-size distribution characterization from single-shot x-ray diffraction using hierarchical Bayesian multi-emitter analysis
papers.abstract: The distribution of grain sizes in a polycrystalline material can be determined from a 2D x-ray diffraction pattern by counting and characterizing diffraction spots, so long as the spots are discrete. This approach breaks down if there is substantial overlap of the reflections due to either a large number of grains in the scattering volume or crowding of spots caused by crystallographic texture. As a result, the spot-counting approach to grain size determination is infeasible for many situations of practical interest. We address this limitation by applying hierarchical probabilistic learning using a reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo framework to jointly infer diffraction spot populations and their intensity distributions. Using synthetic diffraction patterns, we show how this hierarchical model allows recovery of diffraction peak intensities across a wide variety of grain-size distributions and crystallographic textures. From the recovered peak intensities we infer grain-size distributions themselves and characterize the regimes of grain size and texture for which this approach is practical. Finally, we demonstrate the application of our technique by comparing grain-size distributions in Cu-Ti alloy specimens obtained from 2D x-ray diffraction patterns with those from electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). This method of grain-size distribution determination is expected to be particularly useful in the context of high-throughput experimentation, where the minimal sample preparation requirements and short exposure times of single-shot x-ray diffraction are substantial advantages relative to microscopy techniques.

papers.title: Atomic-scale assembly of sulfur vacancy complexes for tailored in-gap states in monolayer WS$_{2}$
papers.abstract: Atomic-scale defects in two-dimensional semiconductors are quasi-isolated quantum systems with promise for emerging technologies. Although their potential as spin qubits, quantum sensors and single-photon emitters has been demonstrated experimentally, creating them deterministically and identifying them chemically remains challenging, which limits control over their electronic states. In this work we assemble sulfur vacancies in monolayer WS$_{2}$ into complexes of different sizes and geometries using the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope. We study their electronic properties by a combination of scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory, revealing the intricate influences of geometry, underlying point group symmetries and spin-orbit coupling on hybridized states. Among the realized sulfur vacancy complexes, we characterize two configurations that are candidates for bright single photon emitters. Our findings demonstrate an atomic-scale method for engineering quantum states within the band gap of two-dimensional semiconductors.

papers.title: Computing $F$-Symbols from Modular Data
papers.abstract: We present a strategy for computing the $F$-symbols of unitary modular categories with a self-dual simple generator, starting from their modular data, which almost entirely avoids the non-linear solution of the pentagon equations. The algorithm climbs a ladder of braid group representations on successively more strands of the generator until enough $F$-symbols have been determined to propagate them to a complete solution. The strategy presented is successful in difficult cases through ranks 11 and 12, including $\operatorname{Z}(\mathrm{Haagerup}_3)$, and does not require the category to be multiplicity-free. Although the algorithm is implemented numerically, we describe a reliable means of recovering the exact $F$-symbols, assuming that in some gauge they lie in a given number field, and of certifying every pentagon and hexagon equation exactly. The exotic rank-11 anisotropic modular category B11-00119 (https://anyonatlas.org/data/B11-00119), with largest fusion coefficient 4, is used as a motivating example, for which the solve takes roughly 10 minutes on a laptop. We will continue to add $F$-symbol solutions to https://AnyonAtlas.org as they are completed.

papers.title: Learning the Anyon Atlas
papers.abstract: We extend our previous search for the modular data of topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions from 22 to 42 anyons, identifying 150,679 new modular data. We do so by adding to our algorithm three rejection gates, two of them based on logistic regression, that discard representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ unlikely to yield modular data. We estimate that roughly 80% of the modular data between ranks 23 and 42 has been identified after closing under known constructions. With this data, we find counterexamples to a conjecture of Geiko and Moore that the reality of the higher Gauss sums suffices for time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories, and propose a refined criterion. We demonstrate the scalability of this gated implementation by identifying prime modular data at rank 100 that is not realized by any Chern-Simons theory. The identified data through rank 42 has been made available at https://AnyonAtlas.org, to which further data will be added as it is found.

papers.title: On the asymmetry polynomial of Schubert varieties
papers.abstract: Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group with length function $\ell$ and longest element $w_0$. For $w\in W$, let $P_w(q)$ be the Poincaré polynomial of the Schubert variety $X_w$. We introduce its asymmetry polynomial $D_w(q):=q^{\ell(w)}P_w(q^{-1})-P_w(q)$. Let $n\geq4$ and $W=S_n$ or $W(B_n)$. For $w\in W$ whose Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomial $P_{\mathrm{id},w}(q)$ satisfies $P_{\mathrm{id},w}(1)=2$, we prove the sharp bound $[q^k]D_w(q)\leq[q^{k-1}]P_{w_0}(q)$ for $1\leq k<\ell(w)/2$. For every $n\geq3$ and $1\leq h\leq2n-4$, we construct an element $b=b_h^n\in W(B_n)$ with $P_{\mathrm{id},b}(q)=1+q^h$, and determine the asymmetry polynomial $D_b(q)$ and all Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials $P_{x,b}(q)$ for $x\leq b$.

papers.title: Counting $6$-Cliques in $O(n^{5.97})$ time and $O(\log n)$ space
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm that, given read-only access to the adjacency matrix of an $n$-vertex graph $G$, computes the number of $6$-cliques in $G$ using $O(n^{5.97})$ time and $O(\log n)$ space. We achieve this by exploiting a decomposition of an equality indicator function underlying, among others, the refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis by OpenAI and Anthropic, and of the $k$-Clique Conjecture by Vassilevska Williams and Zamir [arXiv, 2026]. Via known reductions, this implies an $O(1.994^n)$ time and polynomial space algorithm for Max Cut on $n$-vertex graphs.

papers.title: Instability of layered two-phase flow in a vertical plane channel
papers.abstract: The equilibrium two-phase flows in a vertical plane channel are explored by adopting an approximate Boussinesq-like model. The class of stationary parallel flows examined in this paper features three-layer configurations in which the central core is less dense than the peripheral layers. Such flows are considered purely buoyant, induced by the density difference between the phases. The simplified scheme leads to a formulation where the parameters driving the transition to linear instability of the equilibrium flow are the Archimedes number and the dimensionless positions of the interfaces between the phases. The analysis takes into consideration symmetric and asymmetric flows, including, as special cases, also two-layer configurations with one phase close to the left-hand boundary wall and the other close to the right-hand wall. In particular, the completely antisymmetric flow, where the equilibrium velocity profile is an odd function of the transverse coordinate, shows up as the least stable configuration among those examined in this study.

papers.title: On Hilbert's tenth problem for number fields
papers.abstract: Given a quadratic number field $K$ we show that the $abc$ conjecture over $K$ implies that $\mathbb{Z}$ is Diophantine in $K$ and, hence, a negative answer to Hilbert's tenth problem over $K$. More generally, the same conclusions hold for an arbitrary number field $K$ provided that the $abc$ conjecture holds over $K$ and that there is an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose rank is positive and does not increase over $K$.

papers.title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation
papers.abstract: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow this gap, we introduce three physically motivated augmentations of training data. Two improve generalization, namely exploiting the vehicle's left-right symmetry and emulating accelerometer bias. Combined, they reduce the error on the validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%. Contrary to common expectation, on the SUV the data-driven estimator trained with both augmentations matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same training data.

papers.title: Variation bounds for averages over nondegenerate curves
papers.abstract: In this article, we prove sharp variational estimates for averaging operators over non-degenerate curves in $\R^3.$ The sufficiency follows from dyadic localisation, Sobolev embedding, and local smoothing estimates, and the primary novelty of this article lies in obtaining sharp necessary conditions for variational estimates.

papers.title: Minimal norm of regular vectors in the root lattice of a crystallographic root system
papers.abstract: For a crystallographic root system $Φ$ with Weyl group $W$ and root lattice $L = \mathbb{Z}Φ$, we determine the minimum norm of a vector of $L$ having trivial stabilizer in $W$, and we prove that the vectors attaining it form a single orbit of $W$. Although this is a minimization of a quadratic function over the lattice points of a cone, the minimizer in the dominant chamber is always unique: it is $ρ+ λ$, where $ρ$ is the Weyl vector and $λ$ is $0$ or the minuscule weight in the class of $ρ$ modulo $L$. In particular, the optimal vector is the Weyl vector exactly when the Weyl vector lies in $L$. We give explicit formulas for the families $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$ and $D_n$, with elementary proofs, and the values for the exceptional types $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, $F_4$ and $G_2$. Finally, we explain the coincidences between the minimal norms by the folding of Dynkin diagrams.

papers.title: GenerativeQC: A Generative, GPU-Accelerated Quantum Chemistry Program
papers.abstract: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that computes energies and analytic nuclear forces from Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT) to closed-shell density-fitted CCSD(T) and an MP2-assisted CCSD(T)/complete-basis-set (CBS) composite. Its scientific compiler translates symbolic equations into C++ and CUDA code and uses automatic differentiation to generate the derivative and response programs that analytic forces require. A native runtime executes these programs together with hand-written iterative solvers and integral routines. Across HF and DFT benchmarks for eight methods on water clusters of up to 96 atoms, GenerativeQC is faster than GPU4PySCF in all 128 comparisons on an RTX 5090 GPU and in all but two comparisons on an H100 GPU. For correlated wave functions, compiler-generated derivative contractions and transpose Jacobian operators enable complete density-fitted CCSD(T) and CCSD(T)/CBS analytic forces on GPUs, completing a CCSD(T)/CBS energy-and-force calculation for heptane (23 atoms) in 4.5 min on a single H100 GPU (17 min on RTX 5090).

papers.title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
papers.abstract: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.

papers.title: Comparing Lower and Upper Spectral Gaps of Nonnegative Symmetric Matrices
papers.abstract: We establish sharp estimates comparing the lower and upper spectral gaps of nonnegative symmetric matrices. Combining these comparisons with a multiplicity argument in the spirit of Li and Liu, we improve and extend earlier spectral gap comparison bounds of Saha and Li and Liu, which provide quantitative refinements of an observation of Breuillard, Green, Guralnick and Tao relating combinatorial expansion to two-sided spectral expansion. Our graph estimates hold for nonbipartite even-walk-regular graphs, which covers the classes of graphs, including vertex-transitive graphs, (twisted) Cayley graphs, and (twisted) Cayley sum graphs, investigated in previous work. Under an additional eigenmap assumption, we also establish quantitative two-sided comparisons between the lower and upper spectral gaps. In particular, these comparisons apply to walk-regular graphs.

papers.title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

papers.title: An Upper Bound on the Proportional Choice Number of a Graph
papers.abstract: Proportional choosability is a list analogue of equitable coloring introduced in 2019 that imposes both upper and lower bounds on color class sizes based on the availability of each color. The proportional choice number of a graph $G$, denoted by $χ_{pc}(G)$, is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $G$ is proportionally $k$-choosable. A recently proposed conjecture states that for any graph $G$ with at least one edge, $χ_{pc}(G) \leq Δ(G) + \text{col}(G) - 1$, where $Δ(G)$ is the maximum degree of $G$ and $\text{col}(G)$ is its coloring number. In this paper, we prove this conjecture using a generalization of Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem due to Aharoni and Berger, in which one of the matroids is replaced with an abstract simplicial complex. As a consequence, we can completely determine the proportional choice number of every path: $χ_{pc}(P_1)=1$, $χ_{pc}(P_n)=2$ for $2 \leq n \leq 5$, and $χ_{pc}(P_n)=3$ for $n \geq 6$. This resolves a question about paths that has remained open since the introduction of proportional choosability.

papers.title: Uneven gains in protein-RNA affinity and mutation-effect prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate matched affinities determine mutation effects, but gains in aggregate affinity prediction may transfer unevenly to average effects, ordering and local accuracy. We evaluated eleven method families using method-specific matched populations. Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity mean absolute error from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd. Across 220 mutation pairs from 20 families, it generated stronger responses and improved mean-effect accuracy, with uncertain ranking gains and no decrease in mean centered local error. In an independent external test (24 quantitative pairs from three source-matched families), absolute and ordinary mutation-effect errors fell in all three families. Mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd, with improvements in two families and higher error in one. Error decomposition localized gains in landscape means. PRA-Pred feature tracing, fixed-weight M2-PRNet input controls and matched supervision interventions identified specific restrictions on mutation response. These results establish the need to evaluate average effects, ordering and quantitative local variation jointly.

papers.title: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate
papers.abstract: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

papers.title: Approximate Dynamic Programming with Basis Function Learning
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel approach for approximating the value function in Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our approach is grounded in the approximate linear programming (ALP) framework, wherein basis functions (BFs) play an important role. Traditionally, BFs have been pre-defined, randomly generated, or restricted to specific structures, which both limits the accuracy that can be achieved and leaves no mechanism for improving a given approximation. We instead learn BFs from the model itself, by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate. We introduce the Bellman operator basis function (BOBF) learning method, and prove that each learned BF improves the approximation by a quantifiable amount and that the method converges to the optimal value function. Its shrunken counterpart (SBOBF) retains this guarantee while capping the number of BFs, and therefore the computational effort per iteration. For large-scale problems, where the number of constraints is prohibitive, we develop hybrid variants (HBOBF and SHBOBF) that combine constraint sampling with BF learning, and we show that the improvement and finite-termination guarantees are preserved under explicitly stated conditions. Numerical experiments on (continuous) perishable inventory and queueing control problems demonstrate that our BF learning techniques significantly outperform existing methods in the literature.

papers.title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
papers.abstract: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

papers.title: CratesBump: A Version-Bump Dataset for the Rust Ecosystem
papers.abstract: We release CratesBump, the first public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, together with semver-extract, the tool that builds it. CratesBump is built from every crate on crates.io with at least two releases before 14 September 2026 (about 220,000 crates), giving over two million consecutive release pairs. Each pair has 41 features (code changes from AST diffs, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence, GitHub commit and issue activity), its source repository where listed, and two labels: the literal reading of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and Cargo's rule, under which a 0.y bump is a breaking change. semver-extract regenerates the dataset from public crates.io data and the GitHub API. To illustrate its use we (i) benchmark bump predictors on held-out repositories, finding the task learnable but far from solved, with lower scores on later releases; (ii) measure which feature groups carry the signal; (iii) check, against declared dependency ranges, how often Cargo's rule shields dependents from pre-1.0 breaking releases; and (iv) audit a sample of releases with cargo-semver-checks, finding minor and patch releases that break the public API despite their version number. Dataset and tool are released under open licenses.

papers.title: A disproof of the El-Zahar--Erdős conjecture
papers.abstract: El-Zahar and Erdős asked whether every graph of bounded clique number and sufficiently large chromatic number contains two vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs, each of large chromatic number, with no edge between them. We give a negative answer even for triangle-free graphs. For every integer $g \ge 4$, we show by a probabilistic argument that there exist graphs of girth at least $g$ and arbitrarily large chromatic number in which any two vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs that each require at least seven colors are joined by an edge.

papers.title: Infrared spectrum of the Type Iax supernova remnant Pa30
papers.abstract: The central star of Pa30 and its nebulosity offer one of the best opportunities to study a SN Iax explosion and its remnant. Pa30 is thought to be the product of the historical supernova explosion of 1181. No infrared spectroscopy of its extremely hot central star has hitherto been reported. Here, we present a 0.75-5 $μ$m spectrum taken by the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), together with ground-based infrared spectra, at higher resolution, covering the 0.8-2.5 $μ$m region. The spectra contain very broad lines, which we have attempted to identify and model using the codes CMFGEN and CLOUDY. The CMFGEN modelling suggests that most of the lines are due to OVI. However, CLOUDY modelling, using expected theoretical abundances for the bound remnants of SN Iax explosions, provides evidence for the presence of coronal lines of Si, S, Mg, and Al arising from a shocked gas. This strengthens the suggestion that Pa30 is indeed the remnant of a SN Iax explosion.

papers.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
papers.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

papers.title: Slope stability for normal varieties
papers.abstract: In this expository paper, we review the theory of slope stability of torsion-free sheaves with respect to nef curve classes and extend it to normal varieties.

papers.title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

papers.title: Finite-temperature effects on the single-particle Green's function of a mobile impurity in a Luttinger liquid
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of a quadratically-dispersing quantum impurity interacting through a contact density-density term with a one-dimensional (1D) superfluid described by Luttinger liquid theory. By means of a field-theoretical approach based on the linked-cluster expansion, we quantitatively address the effects of a finite temperature of the 1D bath on the momentum-space single-particle Green's function. Through a careful identification of the resonant phonon-impurity scattering processes, we obtain asymptotic large-time estimates for the thermally-induced exponential damping of the zero-temperature signal both in the $\textit{quasiparticle}$ regime, dominated by the presence of a finite lifetime for the host impurity, and in the $\textit{infrared-dominated}$ regime, where the impurity causes a Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe of the 1D bath. In both cases, we identify a temperature-induced coherence time that sets the characteristic timescale of the exponentially-decaying finite-temperature correction to the amplitude of the zero-temperature single-particle Green's function. Moreover, we draw connections between the aforesaid thermal timescale and the microscopic parameters of the Lieb-Liniger model, which admits an effective Luttinger-liquid description, highlighting the dependence of the inverse coherence time on the intra-bath interactions across the different dynamical regimes of the impurity.

papers.title: Large deviation principles for component counts in the dense regime
papers.abstract: This paper develops large deviation principles for component counts in dense random geometric graphs. We consider a homogeneous Poisson point process on the flat \(d\)-dimensional torus and study the number of isolated components of fixed order \(k\) at connection radii above the connectivity scale. Two types of large deviation behaviour are investigated. First, we prove a Donsker--Varadhan large deviation principle in the regime where the expected number of such components tends to infinity. Second, we study the opposite extreme regime, where this expectation tends to zero, and establish fixed order tail measure limits for the associated \(k\)-component isolation-volume point process. As a consequence, we obtain functional large deviations for the moving threshold component count process.

papers.title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
papers.abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

papers.title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

papers.title: Generalization of Text Line Segmentation for HTR in Historical Documents
papers.abstract: In this paper we investigate the generalization capability of state-of-the-art object detection models (Hi-SAM, YOLO, and RT-DETR) for the automatic segmentation of text lines in historical documents. Generalization is needed because it is not practical for museums and archives to produce large amounts of labeled samples for each new collection. We also evaluate the few-shot setting by fine-tuning the networks with only a small number of training samples per target dataset. To this end, we use nine different datasets that differ significantly in visual layout and language. Additionally, we discuss why mean average precision (mAP), a classic evaluation metric for object detection, is insufficient for assessing the quality of a text line segmentation model. Depending on the dataset, our CRNN models achieve character error rates (CER) ranging from 2.48% to 7.07% per page for the segmented text lines. This is sufficient for reading comprehension and simple text searches. Finally, we quantify the resource and time requirements of training and inference in different use case settings. This forms the basis for more informed decisions about model and hardware choices based on available resources.

papers.title: An Atiyah--Hirzebruch to Adams map and the hastened Adams spectral sequence for supercohomology
papers.abstract: We construct a map of filtered spectra inducing a map from the Atiyah--Hirzebruch spectral sequence (AHSS) to the Baker--Lazarev Adams spectral sequence of a $\mathit{ko}$-module $M$. Using this and a theorem of Bruner--Rognes, we construct a hastened Adams spectral sequence (HASS) for the Postnikov truncations of $\mathit{ko}$ and the connective Adams summand. Then, motivated by questions in quantum field theory, topological phases of matter, and tensor category theory, we apply the HASS to supercohomology, the cohomology theory $I_{\mathbb{C}^\times}(τ_{\le 2}\mathit{ko})$, and observe that in examples of interest it is easier to calculate with than either the AHSS or the usual Adams spectral sequence. We include a User's Guide to the HASS and several worked examples, as well as hastened Adams charts for many commonly encountered $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules.

papers.title: On a Secretary Problem with Two Equal-Sized Pools of Candidates
papers.abstract: This paper presents the solution of a secretary type problem where the decision maker observes a sequence of offers of two types. There are N objects of both types and these objects appear to the decision maker in random order. Objects can only be compared when they are of the same type. The objects of a given type that have already appeared can be ranked according to a complete order. Objects of different types are not comparable. On the appearance of an object, the decision maker must decide whether to accept that object (and thus stop searching) or irrevocably reject it (and thus continue searching). The goal of the decision maker is to accept an object that is the best of its type. The authors present the general form of the optimal policy and the asymptotical solution. The authors give a strong result describing whether an object of relative rank one should be accepted when the same number of objects of both types have been seen.

papers.title: Multi-Band Galaxy Novel-View Synthesis with Radiative Gaussian Fields
papers.abstract: We propose a novel view synthesis tool for galaxies based on Gaussian Splatting (GS). Unlike RGB data, where GS has achieved success, galaxy observations consist of multi-band signals from a massive number of bodies, contain complex patterns of cross-band interactions, and capture light propagation in highly heterogeneous media. As a result, the underlying physical process poses great challenges in model representation and optimization, which have not been investigated in existing research. To this end, we propose a physically inspired Gaussian Splatting method, GalaxyGS, which is equipped with physically meaningful components that capture both the energy emission mechanism of different astronomical bodies and the light propagation between them. In the absence of directly comparable baseline methods, we adopt a wide range of possible alternative approaches. Comparisons conclusively demonstrate that GalaxyGS is better in accuracy and physical fidelity across datasets and metrics.

papers.title: Proof-Relevant Interpolation for Circular Proofs in Linear Logic
papers.abstract: First introduced for proving Craig's interpolation theorem, Maehara's method provides a constructive, proof-theoretic procedure for extracting interpolants in sequent calculus proofs. Building on this method, Saurin developed a ``proof-relevant'' interpolation theorem for first-order linear logic, in the sense that the interpolated proof is obtained by cut-introduction steps that can be reversed via cut-elimination. In this work, we extend Saurin's proof-relevant interpolation to linear logic proofs with cuts as well as to circular proofs in linear logic with fixed-points. We specifically show how Maehara's method can be extended in a proof-relevant way to work on non-cut-free and non-well-founded (but regular) proof objects, and guarantee that the interpolation procedure preserves strong validity. We also study conditions under which one can interpolate system L terms that are not necessarily in normal form.

papers.title: Induction Head Origins of SLAM-ASR Speech Recognition Models
papers.abstract: What makes a small trained map from encoder states to the embedding space of a frozen language model sufficient for competitive speech recognition? The premise of the SLAM-ASR architecture is that a frozen language model possesses linguistic knowledge rich enough to perform the recognition task. This assumption, while reasonable, provides little insight into the mechanisms underlying these models. We therefore seek the concrete internal structures on which they rely. This work shows that SLAM-ASR models rely on induction heads of the frozen language model: the same heads that copy repeated token sequences in text are also important for mapping speech embeddings to transcript tokens. Moreover, we find pairs of heads that behave as a constrained form of differential attention, cancelling attention noise and sharpening attention onto the previously generated word. Finally, we show how induction heads could be used to improve transcription quality under noisy audio.

papers.title: Balanced Simplicial Complexes for the $γ$-Vectors of Zig-Zag Eulerian Polynomials
papers.abstract: In this paper, we construct a simplicial complex whose $f$-vector equals the $γ$-vector of the descent polynomial of an arbitrary canonically labeled rank-one poset. As an application, we prove Petersen and Zhuang's conjecture that the $γ$-vector of the normalized zig-zag Eulerian polynomial is the $f$-vector of a balanced simplicial complex.

papers.title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
papers.abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/

papers.title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
papers.abstract: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $μ$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.

papers.title: On automorphisms of symplectic varieties acting trivially on the second cohomology group
papers.abstract: We prove that the group of automorphisms acting trivially on the torsion-free part of the integral second cohomology on a primitive symplectic variety is a locally trivial deformation invariant. We exhibit some examples of this invariant.

papers.title: The Lyapunov and uniform spectra
papers.abstract: The \textit{Lyapunov spectrum} of a linear cocycle (or vector bundle) is the set of Lyapunov vectors with respect to all ergodic probability measures for the base topological dynamical system. This spectrum disregards trajectories that are atypical from the measure-theoretic viewpoint, and so it is in general insufficient to determine important properties of the cocycle, such as existence of dominated splittings. We resolve this deficiency by introducing a larger set which we call the \textit{uniform spectrum} of the cocycle. This definition is akin to Misiurewicz and Ziemian's rotation set. We prove several properties of the Lyapunov and uniform spectra, including relations between them. Motivated by a theorem of DeWitt and Gogolev, we consider Hölder-continuous cocycles over hyperbolic homeomorphisms and then provide bounds for the uniform spectrum in terms of the Lyapunov spectrum. We exhibit additional connections to the literature.

papers.title: Interpersonal trust, institutional trust and trust in technology in Air Traffic Control
papers.abstract: Air traffic control (ATC), the safe, orderly and efficient management of planes through controlled airspace is a complex task. In this article, we explore the roles that different kinds of trust play in ATC. Our study provides the essential foundations for examining the conditions that need to be satisfied if Air Traffic Controllers are to establish and sustain trust relationships with technical innovations, such as agent-based systems, and so ensure their safe and dependable embedding within ATC work.

papers.title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
papers.abstract: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

papers.title: Low-dimensional optimal stopping with rank-dependent loss
papers.abstract: Sequential selection problems with independent observable scores and rank-dependent objectives are not reducible, in general, to dynamic optimisation over a state space of fixed dimension. We consider optimal stopping problems with truncated loss structures through the lens of the planar Poisson process, where self-similarity removes the time variable and the state is reduced to the $m$ lowest scores observed so far, rescaled to the initial time. For $m=1$ the optimal rule stops at the first record below a hyperbola, which is found by a sliding-window argument. For $m=2$ we derive the equations for the boundaries of the stopping sets of $1$-records and $2$-records, solve them explicitly on a part of the state space, and express the optimal values by quadratures. The value function and the optimal strategy are characterised by a static integro-differential equation. The optimal strategies are compared with simple low-parameter rules, which are close to optimality.

papers.title: Flexibility for the Monge-Ampere system implies flexibility for isometric immersions into Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: We prove that any flexibility result for the Monge-Ampère system implies the corresponding flexibility result for the isometric immersion system, with the same Hölder regularity. We treat the general isometric immersion system, in which both the source and the ambient metrics are arbitrary Hölder regular, in arbitrary dimension and codimension. Combining this implication with existing results for the Monge-Ampère system, we obtain new ${C}^{1,α}$ flexibility statement for isometric immersions with arbitrary source and ambient metrics. To our knowledge, these are the first such results for non-Euclidean ambient metrics.

papers.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
papers.abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

papers.title: The magical memory cost of entanglement spectrum compression
papers.abstract: How much quantum memory is needed to faithfully retain the entanglement spectrum of a bipartite pure state after separating out Bell pairs through local unitaries? We derive the exact tradeoff between Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries, defining an operational measure of entanglement-spectrum complexity. Smoothed entanglement spread bounds this memory cost from below, while diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity. Chaotic circuit dynamics exhibit a transient memory peak whose height increases with system size, followed by declining cost despite continued entropy growth. A large typical Haar-random state requires only an accuracy-dependent memory, whereas stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain a growing cost with size. In the circuits studied, the multiscale spectral structure associated with entanglement catalysis also has a practical consequence for matrix product state compression, yielding a multiplicative overhead not captured by the conventional entropy-based bond dimension estimate.

papers.title: The computational complexity of Undirected Vertex Geography with maximum height 3
papers.abstract: The impartial game Undirected Vertex Geography is known to be polynomial time solvable. The variant in which vertices are assigned heights with maximum value m that reduce by 1 whenever the token is moved from that vertex, denoted UIRm, is known to be polynomial time solvable when m=2 and PSPACE-complete when m=4. We solve the open question of the computational complexity of UIR3 by a reduction from Directed vertex geography, and show that the complexity holds when the underlying graph is planar and (a) has degree at most 3, (b) is bipartite with maximum degree 4, or (c) is bipartite with maximum degree 5 and only has heights of 1 and 3.

papers.title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
papers.abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

papers.title: The Long and Winding Pore: Tuning Porosity in Templated Nanoporous Carbons
papers.abstract: Disordered materials pose a recurring challenge for molecular simulation: realistic structural models are often generated through thermal protocols in which several structural descriptors emerge simultaneously and cannot easily be varied independently. Nanoporous carbons constitute a particularly relevant example: pore size, wall order, curvature, and network tortuosity generally emerge as outcomes of the thermal preparation protocol, rather than being independently prescribed structural parameters. Moreover, for practical applications, models of porous materials should ideally exhibit a percolating pore network, capable of supporting end-to-end transport of adsorbed species through the material. To this end, here we introduce a hierarchy of templating strategies, built around a common melt-quench-anneal protocol driven by a machine-learned interatomic potential for carbon, that progressively separates these variables. A rigid cylindrical template interacting with the environment through a tunable Lennard-Jones potential provides independent control over pore size and local wall organization, while leaving the structural disorder of the surrounding carbon matrix essentially unchanged. Generalizing the template to a spring-connected, tortuous backbone further allows pore geometry and curvature to be prescribed without qualitatively altering the local templating mechanism established for the straight pore. Finally, making the template mobile lets the growing carbon network reshape it in turn, which sharpens pore boundaries and allows sub-nanometer pore sizes to be targeted precisely, as needed for applications such as supercapacitor electrodes. Ultimately, this approach enables systematic studies of structure-property relationships in porous materials for applications such as energy storage, desalination and gas capture.

papers.title: Can Omni-modal LLMs Understand Spoken Intentions?
papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.

papers.title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game
papers.abstract: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals.
